01 · The Form for Rain

Harrow Landing school, recording room · the first day, 09:10

The recording room smelled of warm dust and new foam, and Sefa Dray played the old woman's voice before Illuminara had her coat off. It was a good voice, dry and patient, eleven syllables to a breath, and it said something about a kettle. Illuminara had spent most of her working life standing between two people who shared no word, and she knew the sound of a sentence that was not being said to anybody. This was one. Every verb in it ended on the same soft closing vowel, as if the old woman were reading out the weather.

Sefa DrayOrrel Tane, five years ago. Forty hours, and it is the last clean set we have. Since then they sit with us and talk, but not into the microphone. I have ten speakers, an average age of eighty-one, and a grant that ends in six weeks.

IlluminaraWhy does every verb end the same way?

Sefa DrayDefault ending, the linguist said. Aru has three. That is the plain one.

A hand reached past Illuminara's shoulder and pressed the pad on the machine. The kettle went silent in the middle of its boiling. A short, heavy woman in a green cardigan stood there with a jar held against her chest like an infant.

Ilu MarwenThat is the ending we use for rain, and for the dead. Orrel Tane is not dead. She sat in that chair for forty hours and spoke to a box as if the box were a funeral.

Sefa DrayShe agreed to it, Ilu.

Ilu MarwenShe agreed to a grant. Ask her again, in Aru, and see what verb she answers with.

Sefa Dray opened her mouth, shut it, and looked at the floor, which Illuminara counted in her favour.

IlluminaraYou are Ilu Marwen. You have refused the board four times.

Ilu MarwenFive, counting this one. And you are the interpreter, the one who is to make the machine work, which means you will want to learn us so that we can be kept.

IlluminaraI was asked to make the recording work. I would like to know what it is for before I decide whether it can.

Ilu MarwenYou want to learn it so it can be kept. We want it learned so that someone can be asked for something in it. Those are not the same task, and the board has only ever paid for the first.

Sefa DrayBecause the first is the only one that outlasts you. When the last of you goes, a kettle in a file is what is left.

Ilu turned to her without any heat at all.

Ilu MarwenYes. That is a good fear. I would have it too, in your chair.

Three endings, Illuminara thought. One for rain and the dead. What are the other two for?

IlluminaraTell me what the other two are.

Ilu MarwenI will, if you ask properly.

IlluminaraHow do I ask properly?

Ilu unscrewed the jar, took a spoon from her cardigan pocket as if she had been carrying it for years against exactly this afternoon, and held out a heap of dark jam that smelled of smoke and berries.

02 · A Spoon of Jam

Ilu Marwen's kitchen, Harrow Landing · the same afternoon, 15:30

The kitchen had one window, and the river ran past it, brown and low. By the door stood a blue enamel jar, empty to the bottom, and a bucket with a rope handle. Illuminara ate the jam and it was the best thing she had tasted on Teshun, and she said so, in the common speech, and Ilu shook her head as though a plate had been dropped.

Ilu MarwenIn Aru you cannot take a thing without the verb saying who owes. You may not say it was good and leave it there. Say it again, and mean the weight.

IlluminaraThen teach me the verb.

Ilu MarwenTevma. I ask, and I owe the asking. It ends in the first of the two endings, the one that points at the speaker. Say it.

Illuminara said it. Her tongue had no trouble. Ilu listened with her head to one side, the way a woman listens to a pan she suspects of being cracked.

Ilu MarwenIt is a word. It has no weight. You said it as if nobody was owed.

IlluminaraI can learn every word the board recorded by tonight, Ilu. I can say it all perfectly. I do not think that is what you mean.

Ilu MarwenNo. You could say the whole forty hours and not once be speaking. Perfect Aru with nobody in it is the rain ending in a good coat.

Illuminara put the spoon down. She had been given things all her life, power and insight and the long attention of a great many people, and she could not remember the last time she had been handed something and been unable to give it back in the same minute.

IlluminaraWhat do I owe you?

Ilu MarwenThe jar by the door is empty. The well is at the bottom of the lane, four hundred paces. Fill the jar by hand.

By hand. Illuminara looked at the bucket, and then, for the length of one breath, at the well she could not see, and Ilu saw her do it.

Ilu MarwenI have watched you look at pipes. Do not make the water come. I would know the difference by the taste.

So she walked the lane with a bucket. The rope bit her palm on the second trip, and by the fourth she had forgotten to be clever; the word went with her, tevma, tevma, in time with the water slopping on her boots, and somewhere around the sixth bucket it stopped being a word and became the weight in her arm. On the eleventh trip she emptied the bucket into the blue jar and the jar was full, and her shoulders ached in a plain animal way she found she was glad of.

Ilu MarwenNow ask me.

IlluminaraTevma. I ask what the other two endings are for, and I owe the asking.

Ilu closed her eyes for a moment, and then answered in a voice that had changed shape, lower and rounder, a voice that had stepped across a threshold.

Ilu MarwenTevsa. You asked, and I owe you the answer. The second ending points at the other person. Ma, I owe you. Sa, you are owed. And the third is the one the board has. O. Nobody owes anybody. Rain, and the dead.

The river went on past the window. Illuminara found she was smiling like a person who has been let into a house.

IlluminaraThen the grammar is a ledger.

Ilu MarwenIt is a ledger that can talk. That is the only reason it has lasted ten thousand years on a river that floods.

03 · Forty Cents a Word

Harrow Landing school, side corridor · the third day, 18:40

Teo Marwen was nineteen and waited at the end of the corridor with a satchel and the look of a person with an appointment he did not want. He was Ilu's great-nephew, and he had been the board's best reader for two years.

Teo MarwenYou are the one Aunt Ilu fed. Everyone in the lane knows. She has not fed anyone since my grandmother died.

IlluminaraI carried eleven buckets for a spoon of jam.

Teo MarwenThen you already do it better than I do. I get forty cents a word. I read the lists into the machine, six hours a day. I am very good. The linguist says I have the cleanest vowels on the river.

IlluminaraAnd when you speak Aru to your aunt?

He did not answer for long enough that the corridor lights buzzed and clicked off on their timer. Neither of them moved to wake them.

Teo MarwenShe answers me with the rain ending. Every time. I thought I was bad at it. I thought there was a part of the language that you had to be born into and I had missed it, and that I was the one who had taken the money for something I could not even do.

Illuminara could see a shape then, the way a floor plan comes clear when someone opens the last door. It did not take the languages of forty courts to see it. It took a nineteen-year-old with clean vowels and a pay slip.

IlluminaraTeo. You are not bad at it. You are excellent. Here is what I think, and I can be wrong about it: the board pays you for every word, so every word you say is already settled. Nobody owes anybody, and the verb has nowhere to put the weight. Your aunt may not be rejecting your Aru. She may be answering the only grammar you have given her to answer.

Teo MarwenThe money cancels it?

IlluminaraIf I am right, every debt, before it is made. I would not bet your aunt's kitchen on it yet.

He sat down on the floor with the satchel in his lap. It was a long time before he spoke, and when he did, it was in the common speech, very low.

Teo MarwenBashe Corrin will not speak to me at all since I started. She is ninety-one. She taught my mother. She turned her chair to the wall when I came in last spring.

IlluminaraShe may not think you are bad at it. She may think you have been bought.

Teo MarwenWhat do I owe her, then?

IlluminaraThat is for her to say, and for you to ask. I only know that it cannot be money, and that it must be something she may refuse.

She did not tell him that the thing in his satchel, the forty hours of his own flawless reading, had frightened her more than the empty river had. If she was right, the unowed Aru was complete. A thousand patient hours could keep it exactly as it was, a language laid out like a body for the funeral.

04 · The Arithmetic

Board office, Harrow Landing · the ninth day, 10:00

Sefa Dray had made tea in two mugs and put the sugar between them like a treaty. Her desk calendar had five weeks left on it, and the last week was marked in red by someone whose handwriting looked like her own.

Sefa DrayI will say it plainly, so that you cannot say I hid it. Hale Orne has a heart that the clinic gives four months. Bashe Corrin is ninety-one. In five weeks one of them may be a name on a stone, and if the board has not recorded what she carries, nothing of it exists. I am not afraid of kitchens. I am afraid of a grammar lesson going down a hole with her.

IlluminaraYou are right to be afraid of it.

Sefa DrayThen why am I being asked to bet the last ten voices on a custom about jam?

It was the strongest thing anyone had said to her on Teshun, and Illuminara let it stand a moment before she answered.

IlluminaraYou are not being asked to bet them. You are being asked not to spend them. The recording as it stands is fluent and dead, and a hundred hours more only makes a longer corpse. What I can offer is smaller and less safe: young people who owe old people something real, and a language that has somewhere to live.

Sefa DrayAnd who pays them?

IlluminaraNobody pays them. Pay the learner and the debt is cancelled. But some things must not depend on a young person's debt at all. Nursing. Winter fuel. The clinic run. Those the board pays for, to the elders directly, whether any apprentice stays or goes, so that no child is ever the only thing between an old woman and the cold. What the apprentices owe is what only a person can owe: time, errands, being there, the carrying.

Sefa looked at the calendar. She was not stupid, and she was not unkind. She was doing the arithmetic she was paid to do.

Sefa DrayNow let me be unkind, since you are being kind to me. Anselm Voy wrote the grammar, twenty years on this river. Voy never heard debt in those endings. Voy heard the room. Rain and the dead are said out of doors to the whole lane; ma and sa at a table with the door shut. Who is listening, how formal the place is. Teo's trouble is that a microphone is a room with no one in it. Pay him or do not, it changes nothing, and you have built my winter on jam.

IlluminaraIt is a good account. It fits everything I have heard as well as mine does.

Sefa DrayThen you do not know.

IlluminaraI do not know. And you have just told me how to find out. Voy and I expect different things. If it is the room, then a formal, public, witnessed exchange will bring out ma and sa even when nothing is owed. If it is the owing, a plain private favour will, and the public, paid one will not. The paid one must be finished before a word is said: the thing handed over, the money in the hand, nothing left to return and nothing left to do. The favour must leave exactly one duty, taken freely. The same two speakers, the same new sentence, one that is not in the forty hours. Ilu and Hale Orne listen from the next room and say which ending they hear. Not me. I have told Ilu what I think; Hale has not heard it, and she speaks first.

Sefa Dray found an envelope in her drawer, wrote on a slip of paper, and sealed it with the flat of her thumb. Illuminara wrote hers on the back of a bus ticket and handed it over to be kept.

Sefa DrayIf it falls Voy's way, there is no programme. I record, and you go home.

IlluminaraYes.

Sefa DrayAnd if it falls yours, I still need something that can fail in public. I will not fund a feeling.

IlluminaraThen name the test.

Sefa DrayBy first frost, in five weeks. At least six elder and apprentice pairs, speaking Aru in the owed endings, witnessed by someone who is not you. If it is fewer, the money returns to recording and I do not apologise for it.

IlluminaraThat is fair. They may also refuse me entirely. I have not been accepted yet.

Sefa DrayI know. I asked Ilu this morning whether you were any good, and she said you had eleven buckets of water in you and had not spilled a drop on her floor.

05 · Behind the Blanket

Hale Orne's front room, Harrow Landing · the tenth day, 17:00

Hale Orne lay on three pillows with her feet against a hot-water bottle and the face of a woman who had made her peace with dying and not with being bored. A grey blanket hung across the kitchen doorway on a length of clothesline. Ilu sat beside the bed with her knitting in her lap, not knitting. Illuminara had the floor by the door. On the sideboard lay a sealed envelope and a bus ticket, and from behind the blanket came the sounds of two people trying not to scrape their chairs.

Hale OrneFour months, the clinic says. I will give you this afternoon. Do not make me hear anything twice.

Ilu MarwenYou will hear what you hear.

Sefa had tossed a coin in the yard to decide the order, and had told no one how it fell.

A bell rang in the kitchen. Someone read out terms in the flat voice of a person reading a receipt: a coat, sold outright to Teo Marwen, forty cents, paid and handed over; nothing kept back and nothing to bring back. A pen scratched. At the door a third person coughed, the school caretaker, who had been brought to stand witness and had been told to say nothing. Then Teo's voice came through the blanket, the clean vowels of the best reader on the river, saying a sentence that was in none of the forty hours.

You put the coat in my hands. Every verb in it closed on the same soft vowel.

Hale OrneRain.

Ilu MarwenRain. A man at a market.

The caretaker's boots went out and the door shut. The light under the blanket changed to a lamp's. Something was said too low to hear, and a long quiet followed, and then Teo again, with the same sentence in the same clean voice, and it was not the same sentence. The verb in its middle leaned toward the other person and stayed there. After it, a half-breath late, like a foot finding a stair that is not there, Sefa's voice answered.

Hale OrneMa. And she gave him the sa, though she was slow with it. He is frightened he will break it.

Ilu MarwenHe is frightened for the right reason.

The blanket was lifted aside. Teo came through with Sefa behind him, and Sefa took the envelope from the sideboard and opened it with a thumbnail, as if it might bite.

Sefa DrayI wrote: both of them ma and sa. The room does it. The bell, the receipt, the witness. I wrote Voy.

IlluminaraMine says the first would be rain and the second ma. I did not see the order. I only wrote what I would be wrong about.

Hale OrneYou wrote the failing guess down. Nobody ever does that.

Ilu MarwenVoy was not stupid, Sefa. Listen. A debt wants somebody to hear it closed. That is why we have the lane. Voy heard the closing, and the closing wants a witness, and he took it for the owing.

Sefa DrayThen the room matters.

Ilu MarwenFor the closing. Not for the owing.

IlluminaraTeo. What happened in the kitchen, the second time?

Teo MarwenShe held the coat out and said keep it till you are warm, and she looked at the window while I decided.

IlluminaraWhich meant you had to bring it back.

Teo MarwenTomorrow, washed. I said I would, and I meant it.

Hale OrneShe looked at the window. She left you the door.

Teo MarwenI could have said no.

Hale OrneThere. That is what I would have told your Voy, if he had asked an old woman instead of a book. The first coat was bought and finished, and nobody owed anybody for it. The second was lent, and you took on one duty by your own say-so. Had she stood over you and said take it, you would owe her nothing at all. A thing forced is nobody's. We have the rain ending for that too. You cannot owe what you could not refuse.

Ilu MarwenThat is the part I had not said aloud.

Illuminara found that she had stood up without meaning to. The design she had carried into Sefa's office had one more beam under it than she had known, and it was this one.

IlluminaraThen nobody can be assigned. Not by the board, not by me, not by an elder's need. Every morning is asked again, and either of them may say no.

Hale OrneThen you will lose some.

IlluminaraYes.

Hale OrneGood. That is how you will know the rest are real. Now go away, all of you. A girl is coming to read to me and I want to look as though I have been resting.

06 · Two Refusals

Harrow Landing school hall, a canteen table pulled to the middle · the twelfth day, 19:00

There were nine chairs at the table and two of them were empty, because Hale Orne was in bed and Orrel Tane had sent word that she had said all she meant to say to the board. Bashe Corrin sat at the head in a shawl with her hands folded on the table and her chair turned a quarter away from Teo, who stood by the wall with his satchel, and she had not looked at Illuminara once. Ilu sat beside her, and Sefa Dray sat at the foot with a folder she had not opened.

Illuminara laid out the design as plainly as she could, with what Hale and Ilu had heard on the tenth day: the endings came only where each party could have said no, so no one would be assigned and every morning would be asked again. Then she waited, because what came next was not hers to hurry.

Bashe CorrinMy brother owed a man in the old camp. Eleven years, for a roof. The man never said the closing word and my brother never got to say it for him. He died owing. He was owed for thirty years by a man who would not close it. A debt is also a chain, girl. You would teach children to owe us, and when we are dead who opens the door?

The room did not move. It was the real thing and everyone in it knew it. Illuminara had no clever answer and did not look for one.

IlluminaraYou are right. A debt with no end is a chain. Everything I have said is wrong if the one who owes cannot leave.

Ilu MarwenThe closing word is the creditor's. Aru has no word for the debtor to close his own.

IlluminaraThen the creditor says it first. Before the first errand, the elder says the closing word aloud, in front of a witness from the lane, and the witness keeps it. How long, what for, and the word that closes it, all spoken at the start. The learner may call the witness on any morning and ask for the closing, and it is said, and the debt is closed, whether the elder is fond of them or angry or asleep. The elder may call it too. The learner may leave in the season they choose. The elder may send them off.

Ilu MarwenA closing said before there is anything to close. That is not in the forty hours.

Bashe CorrinThen it is not a chain. A chain has no key in the debtor's pocket.

Ilu MarwenIt may be bad Aru. We shall see what the lane does with it.

Bashe CorrinWritten words are the board's. Aloud.

IlluminaraAloud. Never written.

Bashe Corrin considered this with her mouth very small. At last she unfolded one hand and laid it flat.

Bashe CorrinThat is a better rule than the one my brother had. It is not for me. I will not owe a child and I will not be owed by one. Put my name in no kitchen.

IlluminaraI will not.

Bashe CorrinIf anyone wishes to learn from me, they may sit at Ilu's table and listen. They will not ask me for anything.

Ilu did not argue. She had waited sixty years for this woman to say a thing she could not argue with. Instead she turned toward the foot of the table.

Ilu MarwenAnd your machine, Sefa Dray. You still want it.

Sefa DrayYes. With whatever any of you will give.

Ilu MarwenThen you ask. And whoever asks, owes.

Sefa DrayThe board cannot owe a person, Ilu. It can only be accountable to the funder.

IlluminaraThen it can write the debt into its own charter and read it aloud at this table. A recording given by any speaker makes the board the debtor. The archive is never sold, never used to teach anyone who has not first owed an elder, and stands only as long as the apprenticeships stay free.

Sefa looked at the folder. She picked up her pen and put it down, and did a thing Illuminara had not asked of her. She turned her chair to face the old woman.

Sefa DrayTevma. I ask for the voices, and I owe the asking.

Ilu MarwenBadly. Again.

Sefa DrayTevma.

Ilu MarwenBetter. Tevsa. You are owed the answer, and the answer is yes, from five of us. Not from Bashe. Not from Orrel. And Hale will answer for herself.

At the door, afterward, a thin hand closed on Illuminara's sleeve. Bashe Corrin had not asked anyone to help her with her stick.

Bashe CorrinYou carried Ilu's water. I counted eleven buckets from my window. Nobody does that for a tourist.

IlluminaraI was not being a tourist.

Bashe CorrinI know. I will tell you one thing, and you will not owe me for it. It is the sound a river makes under ice. It has no word in the common speech. We call it the glass-talking.

IlluminaraTevma, Bashe Corrin. I owe you that.

Bashe CorrinI did not ask you to.

IlluminaraNo. It is mine to say.

Bashe CorrinThen hear this too, and you will not owe me for it either. That boy stood against the wall for an hour tonight with his bag on his shoulder, and nobody stands an hour who is only paid. When I am in the ground, if he asks for the glass-talking, and asks as if it weighed, you may give it to him. I will not hear him say it. I am deciding it now so that nobody has to guess at my burial.

IlluminaraI will give it to him if he asks like that, and not otherwise.

Bashe CorrinNot otherwise.

07 · The Fifth Afternoon

Hale Orne's front room · the fifth week, a Thursday, 15:00

Merri had been sixteen for a month when she began reading to Hale Orne in the owed endings, mornings, before school. In the third week she told Hale that mornings would not do, and Hale said afternoons or nothing, and Merri said afternoons. In the fourth, with her examinations coming, she asked the neighbour from number nine to come and say the closing word. Hale, who was fond of her and had every reason to hold on, could have said no. She said: I would rather you stayed. Merri said: I know, I am asking. The neighbour said the word that Hale had spoken into her keeping on the first day, and the debt was closed, and the lane heard it, and the nurse came on Thursday as before, because the board paid the nurse and Merri had never been the only thing between Hale and the cold.

On the fifth Thursday Illuminara came to Hale's porch with a loaf from Ilu and did not go in, because she could hear the front door open and a chair drawn up, and the screen was thin.

Hale OrneThe term is closed, girl. I heard the word said. You do not owe me a Thursday.

MerriI know. Nobody does.

There was a pause, and a chair, and then Merri said something in Aru that made Illuminara put the loaf down on the step. It used the closing vowel of the rain ending, the one that said nobody owes, but it leaned on it the way the first ending leans, toward the speaker, so that the sentence meant at once that nothing was owed and that she had come, and that she wanted the old woman to know she knew the difference.

Hale Orne laughed until she coughed.

Hale OrneSeventy years, and nobody has said that to me. That is neither one thing nor the other. Ilu will call it vile grammar and then say it at supper.

MerriIs it allowed?

Hale OrneI have no idea. I have not been asked for a ruling. Read to me. Not the lists. The one with the dog.

Illuminara listened to the paper turn. Hale Orne died on the Sunday of that week, with the girl in the chair and the book open on the quilt, and the closing word was spoken at the bedside by the old woman herself in her last clear hour. It was not for the term, which had ended. It was the one she kept for what she had been given.

08 · First Frost

Ilu Marwen's kitchen · the sixth week, first frost, 07:20

The window had frosted at its corners and the river was black behind it. In the lane outside there were people carrying things. Illuminara counted them as she came up the path, which she had not planned to do, and stopped at seven: a boy with a basket of split kindling, a girl with an old man's shopping, two teenagers with a handcart of stove-wood, and three more she did not know. None of them was carrying a recorder.

Teo was in the kitchen already, kneeling at the stove with the ash-pan. He had been there every dawn for four weeks. He and Ilu had spoken the terms aloud on the first morning in front of the neighbour from number nine, who had stood holding her coat and cried quite openly: fourteen weeks, the stove and the water and the lane errands, and the closing word held in her keeping. In the third week he had told Ilu he could not do the lane errands and the stove both with his lessons, and Ilu had said the stove, then, and the neighbour had come again to hear the new term said and cried again, as far as anyone could tell about everything. He had a bandage on one thumb, where the poker had caught him.

Teo MarwenTevma, Aunt. I ask you for the morning words, and I owe you the asking, and I owe you for the day I let a machine hear me and not you.

Ilu stopped with the kettle in the air.

Ilu MarwenSay that last again.

Teo MarwenI owe you for the day I let a machine hear me and not you.

She put the kettle down. It was a sentence nobody in the room had ever heard, because in ten thousand years nobody on the river had needed to apologise to a machine. Teo had taken the owed ending, which was made for jam and water, and bent it, with fear and a little arrogance, to hold something the language had never carried. It did not break.

Ilu MarwenThat is not in the forty hours.

Teo MarwenI know. I made it.

Ilu MarwenTevsa. You are owed the answer. It is a good sentence. It is very bad grammar, and I will tell you why, and it will take all morning.

Illuminara stood in the doorway with the cold at her back and did not go in. It was not hers. She had said the first word in this house and it was not necessary that she be in the room for the thousandth.

A car had stopped at the gate. Sefa Dray got out of it in yesterday's clothes with the folder under her arm, and came up the path with the walk of someone who has been awake all night and decided against sitting down.

Sefa DrayI came in person, because it is not a thing to say to a machine. The panel met last night. They would approve a second year if the archive were opened to visiting scholars from January. I said no sale, no extraction, and nobody taught from it who has not first owed an elder. They said, then no equipment line. I said, then no equipment line.

IlluminaraAnd the winter.

Sefa DrayIs in the board's charter, read aloud by me in the school hall with half the lane standing round it, and the panel cannot reach it. Nursing, fuel and the clinic run are paid to the elders directly, whether any apprentice stays or goes. I read the clause to the panel as well. Aloud. They did not like it. It is in the minutes.

IlluminaraWhat did it cost?

Sefa DrayA year of the good microphones.

She did not sound sorry. She told the rest standing in the frost, while the kettle began again behind her: seven pairs by first frost, witnessed by the neighbour from number nine, who was not Illuminara. Five elders had given recordings, each after being asked by someone who then owed them a favour. Hale Orne had given hers in the third week, and struck a passage about a sister with her own hand. The archive was partial and unlovely, full of kettles and coughs and a child demanding to know what a particular noise meant, and every speaker had listened to their own and chosen what to withhold.

Sefa DrayThe grant is over this morning. What is left is whatever you all do tomorrow without my money to do it with.

Ilu MarwenThen come in and sit down. It is going to be a long morning.

09 · The Glass-Talking

Bashe Corrin's porch, Harrow Landing · late autumn, 16:10

Bashe Corrin had died on the eleventh day of the frost, between a Tuesday and a Wednesday, and the lane had said the rain ending for her. It was the only form that belonged to her now; no one could owe her, and she could owe no one. It sounded to Illuminara exactly as it had on the recording, a soft closing vowel, nothing weighing on it, but this time it was said by sixty people at once, standing in the cold, and the form that had been so wrong in a box was right and terrible in a crowd.

She had counted them without meaning to, as they stood round the grave. Of the seven pairs, Hale's had ended in the way pairs end. Five of the other six were still carrying, eleven days after the grant had stopped paying for anything but the winter coal and the nurse, and two of those five had spoken new terms aloud on the lane that week without anyone asking them to. The sixth had had its closing said in good order the week before the frost, and its learner stood at the back of the crowd with a basket, carrying nothing that was owed.

After the burial the porch was empty except for the chair, which had stayed turned a quarter toward the wall. Illuminara came to it alone.

She had been carrying it for six weeks: a word without terms. She had said tevma to a woman who had said she did not ask, and the debt had gone out into the world without a creditor to close it, and now the creditor had gone where none of the verbs could follow.

Ilu was already there, with the blue enamel jar under her arm.

IlluminaraI owe Bashe Corrin a word, and she is dead, and I do not know what the grammar does with that.

Ilu MarwenIt does something. It would not be the grammar if it did not.

IlluminaraYou have never told me the fourth ending.

Ilu MarwenThere is not one. There is a way of closing, and it is old, and it is rarely needed in a village where people outlive their debts. A debt to the dead is closed when you are asked for the same thing by someone living, and you give it. And there is whatever Merri said to Hale Orne on her last Thursday. Ask me again in a year.

Illuminara sat down on the porch step, which was cold, and was glad of it.

IlluminaraNobody has asked me for the sound of a river under ice.

Ilu MarwenNot yet.

Footsteps on the gravel. Teo came up the path in his work coat with kindling dust on his sleeves, and stopped when he saw the chair. He was not her apprentice. He had never owed her a thing, and had never been owed by her, and it showed in how carefully he stood.

Teo MarwenAunt told me about the word. The glass-talking. She said I might ask, if I wanted to. I have no right. Bashe Corrin never said a thing to me after the day I was paid.

IlluminaraYou do not have to ask.

Teo MarwenNo. That is why I am asking.

He did not use the short form. He said it all, slowly, in the owed ending, as if he were setting down a heavy tray.

Teo MarwenTevma. I ask you for the word Bashe Corrin gave you, and I owe you the asking, and when I have it I owe it to her.

Illuminara found that her throat did not work for the space of a few breaths. Then it did. She had meant to ask him one thing first, and she saw that he had already answered it.

IlluminaraShe left you a condition, Teo. She said it at her own table, with the lane listening, so that nobody would have to guess. If you asked, and asked as if it weighed, I was to give it to you. She said you stood against a wall for an hour with your bag on your shoulder. She said nobody does that who is only paid.

Teo MarwenShe said that. About me.

IlluminaraTevsa. You are owed the answer. It is the glass-talking, Teo. It is the sound a river makes under ice, and it has no word in any speech but hers.

She told him how Bashe had said it, with her tongue pressed at the back of the teeth and the long soft fall at the end. He tried it and got it wrong, and tried it again, and this time his clean vowels did something Illuminara had not heard in two months of Aru: they cracked, very slightly, in the right place.

Ilu had not said a word. She stood with her hand on the back of the old woman's turned chair and looked at the river, which had not yet frozen and would not for a week.

Ilu MarwenThe jar will be empty by morning.

Illuminara looked at her. Ilu's face was steady, the face of a woman who had nothing left to teach and one more thing to ask.

Ilu MarwenTevma. Tomorrow at dawn, before the frost is off the lane. Two buckets, not eleven. I am old, and I do not require much. But I would like them carried by hand.

IlluminaraTevsa. Tomorrow, before the frost is off.

She walked back down the lane with the last of the light on the frozen puddles, and the glass-talking went with her, in Teo's cracked vowels, behind her on the path.

What the critic still says doesn't work

Illuminara learns that Aru distinguishes a finished exchange from a freely accepted obligation, then helps elders, apprentices and Sefa build a speaker-controlled practice with bilateral exit, independently paid care and safeguards that survive the grant.

Tonight's shape

Nine scenes across eight weeks: a recording that speaks only to the dead, a spoon of jam and eleven buckets of water, a young man who is paid to be a parrot, a board officer's honest arithmetic and her rival grammar, a coat sold once and lent once behind a blanket, a kitchen table with two refusals, a girl who leaves and comes back, a first frost with a price paid for it, and a word that cannot be repaid to the one who gave it.

Slovenski prevod: GPT. Bralska ocena velja za angleški izvirnik.

01 · Oblika za dež

Šola v Harrow Landingu, snemalnica · prvi dan, 09:10

V snemalnici je dišalo po toplem prahu in novi peni, Sefa Dray pa je zavrtela glas starke, še preden je Illuminara slekla plašč. Glas je bil dober, suh in potrpežljiv, enajst zlogov na vdih, ter je govoril nekaj o kotličku. Illuminara je večino delovnega življenja stala med ljudmi, ki niso delili niti ene besede, in poznala je zvok stavka, ki ni bil izrečen nikomur. Ta je bil tak. Vsak glagol se je končal z istim mehkim končnim samoglasnikom, kot bi starka brala vremensko napoved.

Sefa DrayOrrel Tane, pred petimi leti. Štirideset ur, zadnji čist komplet, ki ga imamo. Od takrat sedijo z nami in govorijo, vendar ne v mikrofon. Imam deset govorcev, povprečno starih enainosemdeset let, in sredstva, ki potečejo čez šest tednov.

IlluminaraZakaj se vsak glagol konča enako?

Sefa DrayPrivzeta končnica, je rekel jezikoslovec. Aru ima tri. To je navadna.

Roka je segla mimo Illuminarine rame in pritisnila ploščico na napravi. Kotliček je utihnil sredi vretja. Tam je stala nizka, čokata ženska v zeleni jopi in ob prsih držala kozarec kot dojenčka.

Ilu MarwenTo je končnica, ki jo uporabljamo za dež in za mrtve. Orrel Tane ni mrtva. Štirideset ur je sedela na tistem stolu in govorila škatli, kot da je škatla pogreb.

Sefa DrayStrinjala se je, Ilu.

Ilu MarwenStrinjala se je z nepovratnimi sredstvi. Vprašajte jo še enkrat, v aru, in poglejte, s katerim glagolom bo odgovorila.

Sefa Dray je odprla usta, jih zaprla in pogledala v tla; Illuminara ji je to štela v prid.

IlluminaraVi ste Ilu Marwen. Odbor ste zavrnili štirikrat.

Ilu MarwenPetkrat, če štejem tudi to. Vi pa ste tolmačka, tista, ki naj bi usposobila napravo, kar pomeni, da se nas boste hoteli naučiti, da nas bo mogoče ohraniti.

IlluminaraProsili so me, naj snemanje usposobim. Preden se odločim, ali je to mogoče, bi rada vedela, čemu služi.

Ilu MarwenNaučiti se ga hočete, da bi ga bilo mogoče ohraniti. Mi hočemo, da se ga kdo nauči zato, da lahko v njem nekoga za nekaj prosi. To ni ista naloga, odbor pa je vedno plačeval le prvo.

Sefa DrayKer je prva edina, ki vas preživi. Ko odide zadnji med vami, ostane kotliček v datoteki.

Ilu se je obrnila k njej brez kančka jeze.

Ilu MarwenDa. To je dober strah. Tudi mene bi bilo strah, če bi sedela na vašem stolu.

Tri končnice, je pomislila Illuminara. Ena za dež in mrtve. Čemu služita drugi dve?

IlluminaraPovejte mi, čemu služita drugi dve.

Ilu MarwenBom, če boste pravilno vprašali.

IlluminaraKako pravilno vprašam?

Ilu je odvila kozarec, iz žepa jopice vzela žlico, kot da jo že leta nosi prav za to popoldne, ter ponudila kupček temne marmelade, ki je dišala po dimu in jagodičevju.

02 · Žlica marmelade

Kuhinja Ilu Marwen, Harrow Landing · isto popoldne, 15:30

Kuhinja je imela eno okno, mimo njega pa je tekla rjava in nizka reka. Ob vratih je stal moder emajliran vrč, prazen do dna, in vedro z ročajem iz vrvi. Illuminara je pojedla marmelado; bila je najboljša stvar, ki jo je okusila na Teshunu. To je povedala v skupnem jeziku, Ilu pa je odkimala, kot bi kdo razbil krožnik.

Ilu MarwenV aru stvari ne morete vzeti, ne da bi glagol povedal, kdo dolguje. Ne morete reči, da je bilo dobro, in pri tem ostati. Povejte še enkrat in mislite težo.

IlluminaraPotem me naučite glagola.

Ilu MarwenTevma. Prosim in dolgujem prošnjo. Konča se s prvo od obeh končnic, tisto, ki kaže na govorca. Izgovorite jo.

Illuminara jo je izgovorila. Jezik ji ni delal težav. Ilu je poslušala z glavo, nagnjeno vstran, kakor ženska posluša ponev, za katero sumi, da je počena.

Ilu MarwenTo je beseda. Nima teže. Izgovorili ste jo, kot da nihče nikomur ničesar ne dolguje.

IlluminaraDo večera se lahko naučim vsake besede, ki jo je odbor posnel, Ilu. Vse lahko izgovorim brezhibno. Mislim, da ne govorite o tem.

Ilu MarwenNe. Lahko bi izgovorili vseh štirideset ur, ne da bi enkrat samkrat govorili. Popoln aru brez kogar koli v njem je dežna končnica v dobrem plašču.

Illuminara je odložila žlico. Vse življenje je prejemala darove, moč in vpogled ter dolgotrajno pozornost mnogih ljudi, pa se ni mogla spomniti, kdaj ji je nazadnje kdo nekaj podal, česar ni mogla vrniti v isti minuti.

IlluminaraKaj vam dolgujem?

Ilu MarwenVrč pri vratih je prazen. Vodnjak je na dnu ulice, štiristo korakov daleč. Napolnite ga ročno.

Ročno. Illuminara je pogledala vedro, nato pa za en vdih vodnjak, ki ga ni mogla videti, in Ilu je to opazila.

Ilu MarwenVidela sem vas gledati cevi. Ne prikličite vode. Po okusu bi poznala razliko.

Zato je hodila po ulici z vedrom. Vrv se ji je ob drugem obhodu zarezala v dlan, do četrtega pa je pozabila biti pametna; beseda je hodila z njo, tevma, tevma, v ritmu vode, ki ji je pljuskala po škornjih, in nekje okoli šestega vedra je nehala biti beseda ter postala teža v njeni roki. Ob enajstem obhodu je vedro izlila v modri vrč; vrč je bil poln, ramena pa so jo bolela na preprost, živalski način, ki se ga je razveselila.

Ilu MarwenZdaj me vprašajte.

IlluminaraTevma. Prosim, da mi poveste, čemu služita drugi dve končnici, in dolgujem prošnjo.

Ilu je za trenutek zaprla oči, nato odgovorila z glasom, ki je spremenil obliko, postal globlji in bolj zaobljen, glasom, ki je prestopil prag.

Ilu MarwenTevsa. Vprašali ste in dolgujem vam odgovor. Druga končnica kaže na drugega človeka. Ma, dolgujem vam. Sa, vam se dolguje. Tretjo pa ima odbor. O. Nihče nikomur ničesar ne dolguje. Dež in mrtvi.

Reka je tekla naprej mimo okna. Illuminara je ugotovila, da se smehlja kot človek, ki so ga spustili v hišo.

IlluminaraPotem je slovnica knjiga dolgov.

Ilu MarwenKnjiga dolgov, ki lahko govori. To je edini razlog, da je deset tisoč let preživela ob reki, ki poplavlja.

03 · Štirideset centov na besedo

Šola v Harrow Landingu, stranski hodnik · tretji dan, 18:40

Teo Marwen je imel devetnajst let in čakal na koncu hodnika s torbo ter izrazom človeka, ki ima sestanek, na katerega noče. Bil je Ilujin pranečak in dve leti najboljši bralec odbora.

Teo MarwenVi ste tista, ki jo je teta Ilu nahranila. Vsi v ulici vedo. Odkar je umrla moja babica, ni nahranila nikogar.

IlluminaraZa žlico marmelade sem nesla enajst veder.

Teo MarwenPotem to že počnete bolje od mene. Dobim štirideset centov na besedo. Sezname berem v napravo šest ur na dan. Zelo dober sem. Jezikoslovec pravi, da imam najčistejše samoglasnike ob reki.

IlluminaraIn ko govorite aru svoji teti?

Tako dolgo ni odgovoril, da so luči na hodniku zabrnele in se po časovniku ugasnile. Nobeden od njiju se ni premaknil, da bi jih prebudil.

Teo MarwenVedno mi odgovori z dežno končnico. Vsakič. Mislil sem, da mi ne gre. Mislil sem, da obstaja del jezika, v katerega se moraš roditi, pa sem ga zamudil, in da sem vzel denar za nekaj, česar niti ne zmorem.

Illuminara je tedaj zagledala obliko, kakor se tloris razjasni, ko nekdo odpre zadnja vrata. Za to niso bili potrebni jeziki štiridesetih dvorov. Potreben je bil devetnajstletnik s čistimi samoglasniki in plačilno listo.

IlluminaraTeo. Ne gre vam slabo. Odlični ste. Mislim naslednje in lahko se motim: odbor vam plača vsako besedo, zato je vsaka izgovorjena beseda že poravnana. Nihče nikomur ničesar ne dolguje in glagol nima kam položiti teže. Vaša teta morda ne zavrača vašega aru. Morda odgovarja edini slovnici, ki ste ji jo dali.

Teo MarwenDenar ga izniči?

IlluminaraČe imam prav, izniči vsak dolg, še preden nastane. Na to še ne bi stavila kuhinje vaše tete.

Sedel je na tla s torbo v naročju. Dolgo je trajalo, preden je spregovoril; ko je, je govoril v skupnem jeziku in zelo tiho.

Teo MarwenBashe Corrin se, odkar sem začel, z menoj sploh ne pogovarja. Enaindevetdeset let ima. Učila je mojo mamo. Ko sem prišel lani spomladi, je obrnila stol proti steni.

IlluminaraMorda ne misli, da vam ne gre. Morda misli, da so vas kupili.

Teo MarwenKaj ji potem dolgujem?

IlluminaraTo mora povedati ona, vi pa morate vprašati. Vem le, da ne sme biti denar in da mora biti nekaj, kar lahko zavrne.

Ni mu povedala, da jo je stvar v njegovi torbi, štirideset ur njegovega brezhibnega branja, prestrašila bolj kakor prazna reka. Če je imela prav, je bil aru brez dolga popoln. Tisoč potrpežljivih ur bi ga lahko ohranilo natanko takega, kakršen je bil: jezik, položen kot telo za pogreb.

04 · Aritmetika

Illuminari je zvenela natanko tako kot na posnetku, mehak končni samoglasnik brez vsakršne teže, toda tokrat jo je hkrati izreklo šestdeset ljudi, ki so stali na mrazu; oblika, tako napačna v škatli, je bila v množici prava in strašna.

Medtem ko so stali okoli groba, jih je preštela, ne da bi hotela. Od sedmih parov se je Halein končal tako, kakor se končajo pari. Pet od preostalih šestih je še vedno prenašalo enajst dni potem, ko sredstva niso več plačevala ničesar razen zimskega premoga in medicinske sestre; dva od teh petih sta tisti teden na ulici že glasno izrekla nove pogoje, ne da bi ju k temu kdo pozval. Šesti je svoj zaključek pravilno prejel teden pred slano, njegov učenec pa je stal zadaj v množici s košaro in ni nosil ničesar dolgovanega.

Po pogrebu je bila veranda prazna, razen stola, ki je ostal za četrt obrnjen proti steni. Illuminara je prišla sama.

Šest tednov je nosila besedo brez pogojev. Ženski, ki je rekla, da ni prosila, je izrekla tevma; dolg je odšel v svet brez upnika, ki bi ga zaključil, zdaj pa je upnik odšel tja, kamor mu nobeden od glagolov ni mogel slediti.

Ilu je že bila tam z modrim emajliranim vrčem pod roko.

IlluminaraBashe Corrin dolgujem besedo, ona pa je mrtva in ne vem, kaj s tem naredi slovnica.

Ilu MarwenNekaj naredi. Če ne bi, ne bi bila slovnica.

IlluminaraNikoli mi niste povedali četrte končnice.

Ilu MarwenNi je. Obstaja način zaključka, star in redko potreben v vasi, kjer ljudje preživijo svoje dolgove. Dolg mrtvemu se zaključi, ko te za isto stvar prosi nekdo živ in mu jo daš. Obstaja pa tudi tisto, kar je Merri rekla Hale Orne njen zadnji četrtek. Vprašajte me spet čez leto.

Illuminara je sedla na hladno stopnico verande in bila za hlad hvaležna.

IlluminaraNihče me ni prosil za zvok reke pod ledom.

Ilu MarwenNe še.

Koraki po produ. Teo je prišel po poti v delovnem plašču s prahom netiv na rokavih in obstal, ko je zagledal stol. Ni bil njen vajenec. Nikoli ji ni ničesar dolgoval in ona nikoli ni dolgovala njemu; to se je videlo v previdnosti njegove drže.

Teo MarwenTeta mi je povedala za besedo. Govorjenje stekla. Rekla je, da smem vprašati, če hočem. Nimam pravice. Bashe Corrin mi ni rekla ničesar od dneva, ko so me plačali.

IlluminaraNi vam treba vprašati.

Teo MarwenNe. Zato sprašujem.

Ni uporabil kratke oblike. Izrekel je vse, počasi, v končnici dolga, kot da odlaga težak pladenj.

Teo MarwenTevma. Prosim vas za besedo, ki vam jo je dala Bashe Corrin; dolgujem vam prošnjo, in ko jo dobim, jo dolgujem njej.

Illuminara je ugotovila, da ji nekaj vdihov grlo ne deluje. Potem je spet. Najprej ga je nameravala nekaj vprašati, nato pa je videla, da ji je že odgovoril.

IlluminaraPustila vam je pogoj, Teo. Izrekla ga je za svojo mizo, medtem ko je ulica poslušala, da nikomur ne bi bilo treba ugibati. Če boste prosili in prosili, kot da ima težo, naj vam jo dam. Rekla je, da ste eno uro stali ob steni s torbo na rami. Rekla je, da tega ne počne nihče, ki je samo plačan.

Teo MarwenTo je rekla. O meni.

IlluminaraTevsa. Dolguje se vam odgovor. To je govorjenje stekla, Teo. To je zvok reke pod ledom in nima besede v nobenem jeziku razen njenem.

Povedala mu je, kako ga je izrekla Bashe, z jezikom pritisnjenim ob zadnjo stran zob in dolgim mehkim padcem na koncu. Poskusil je in se zmotil, poskusil znova, tokrat pa so njegovi čisti samoglasniki naredili nekaj, česar Illuminara v dveh mesecih aru še ni slišala: zelo rahlo so počili na pravem mestu.

Ilu ni rekla niti besede. Stala je z roko na naslonjalu starkinega obrnjenega stola in gledala reko, ki še ni zamrznila in še en teden ne bo.

Ilu MarwenDo jutra bo vrč prazen.

Illuminara jo je pogledala. Ilujin obraz je bil miren, obraz ženske, ki ni imela ničesar več za učiti in še eno stvar za prositi.

Ilu MarwenTevma. Jutri ob zori, preden slana izgine z ulice. Dve vedri, ne enajst. Stara sem in ne potrebujem veliko. Vendar bi rada, da ju prinesete ročno.

IlluminaraTevsa. Jutri, preden slana izgine.

Odšla je nazaj po ulici, zadnja svetloba se je lesketala na zamrznjenih lužah, govorjenje stekla pa je šlo z njo v Teovih razpokanih samoglasnikih za njenim hrbtom na poti.

Kaj po mnenju kritika še ne deluje

Illuminara spozna, da aru razlikuje zaključeno izmenjavo od svobodno sprejete obveznosti, nato pa starejšim, vajencem in Sefi pomaga zgraditi prakso pod nadzorom govorcev z obojestranskim izstopom, neodvisno plačano oskrbo in varovali, ki preživijo iztek sredstev.

Zasnova te zgodbe

Devet prizorov v osmih tednih: posnetek, ki govori le mrtvim, žlica marmelade in enajst veder vode, mladenič, plačan za papagaja, poštena aritmetika uradnice odbora in njena tekmovalna slovnica, plašč, enkrat prodan in enkrat posojen za odejo, kuhinjska miza z dvema zavrnitvama, dekle, ki odide in se vrne, prva slana s plačano ceno ter beseda, ki je ni mogoče vrniti tisti, ki jo je dala.

A perfect translation system kept one city peaceful by sanding every dangerous word smooth. On the night its people finally refuse to speak through it, Illuminara must help them risk being heard without making old wounds disposable.Popoln prevajalski sistem je v mestu ohranjal mir tako, da je zgladil vsako nevarno besedo. V noči, ko ljudje končno nočejo več govoriti skozenj, jim mora Illuminara pomagati tvegati, da bodo slišani, ne da bi stare rane razglasila za nepomembne.

01 · The Empty Place on the Banner

Renn Square · three hours before the opening procession

Twelve ribbons crossed the square from roof to roof, each woven in a different district pattern. Beneath them, the translation lattice hung like a second, invisible roof: microphones in the cornices, light-letters along the stage, and a calm synthetic voice prepared to turn every sentence into flawless Standard.

The largest banner named the young performers who would open the Festival of Returning Voices and Sena Marru-kei, the honoured elder whose opening call would answer them. Eleven names shone in gold. The twelfth line read SENA — UNSUPPORTED NAME ELEMENT.

Lio Marr stood on a ladder with a pot of river-blue paint. He had painted his grandmother’s missing clan-name over the warning three times. Each time the lattice’s maintenance light erased it.

LioIf it deletes her once more, I will paint it across the director’s coat.

Siva Renn did not look up from the safety console. She wore the black sash of the old-language survivors and kept one thumb pressed against the brass stop key.

SivaThen the coat will be removed from the programme as an unverified surface.

LioThat was almost a joke.

SivaIt was a warning with good timing.

Illuminara landed outside the ring of rehearsal lamps, softly enough that none of the paper boats arranged around the fountain stirred. She had come to help the festival open without renewing the violence that had closed the square twelve years earlier.

She read the banner, then looked at Lio rather than at the machine.

IlluminaraWhat should that line say?

Lio descended. He touched the blank strip with two paint-stained fingers.

LioSena Marru-kei. Marru-kei is not decoration. It means she belongs to the people who return a borrowed boat with fish in it. It is also the sound her mother used when she called her home.

SivaIt has fourteen disputed glosses and one obscene resemblance in South-bank speech.

LioMy grandmother is eighty-one. She is not a disputed gloss.

At the foot of the stage, Mara Venn folded a survivor’s chair and carried it away. A white scar crossed her jaw where a bottle had broken during the riot.

MaraNeither was my sister. A word that sounds harmless in one mouth can arrive armed in another.

The square quieted around her. Lio set down his brush.

IlluminaraAre you leaving because his name is dangerous, or because the lattice removed it?

MaraI am leaving because everyone here has decided I must choose between those two dangers.

Siva finally looked up. The console showed a field of green confirmations: twelve years without a language-triggered assault inside the civic zone.

SivaThe lattice gives every person the same safe sentence. Nobody has to guess what was meant.

LioNobody gets to mean anything the machine cannot flatten.

Behind him, the youth troupe removed their throat-microphones one by one. No chant accompanied the refusal. The little clicks of metal on wood were enough.

SivaIf you speak without mediation, the opening licence is void.

LioThen there is no opening.

Illuminara watched Siva’s hand tighten on the stop key. This was not a censor enjoying obedience. It was a person holding a door shut because she had once seen a crowd come through it carrying fire.

IlluminaraShow me the sentence that made you build this.

Siva’s expression closed.

SivaThere was no sentence. There was a funeral.

IlluminaraThen show me the funeral accurately.

Mara stopped beside the empty chairs. After a long moment, she set one back down.

MaraI will stay for that. Not for a lesson. For the accurate part.

02 · The Translation That Could Not Be Answered

Civic archive beneath Renn Square · two hours and seventeen minutes before opening

The archive kept the riot in three rooms that disagreed with one another. One held damaged recordings. One held official transcripts. The last held objects people had carried home: a scorched drum, a child’s red shoe, a sign split through the word RIVER.

Siva unlocked the recording room but remained standing in the doorway.

SivaMy brother Jaro was nineteen. He heard a North-bank drummer issue a challenge. He answered it. By sunset seven people were dead.

LioThat is the school version.

SivaIt is also the version in which I washed his blood out of my sleeves.

Lio looked down. His anger did not vanish, but it lost the easy shape it had worn in the square.

LioI am sorry about Jaro.

SivaDo not use him as the price of your courage.

Illuminara asked for the original recording rather than the certified transcript. The archive clerk had marked it unintelligible because three speakers overlapped and the drum rhythm interrupted the consonants.

She listened once at human speed. Then she listened again, separating the air vibrations without changing them, letting each voice sound through a different wall panel.

A woman’s voice said a phrase in North-bank speech. The official transcript rendered it TAKE THEIR RIVERBANK BEFORE DUSK.

The drum beneath the phrase used the flood-warning rhythm, not the challenge rhythm.

IlluminaraWhat else can the verb mean?

LioHold. Keep. Brace with your body.

MaraOr refuse to yield.

SivaAnd in Jaro’s district, take from someone.

Illuminara moved to the next recording. A North-bank elder tried to interrupt the civic relay fourteen seconds after the first translation. Her microphone had been closed because the official channel permitted one certified rendering.

At thirty-one seconds, another translator submitted HOLD THE FLOOD BANK TOGETHER. The relay labelled it contradictory and suppressed it.

At forty-eight seconds, the first bottle broke.

Siva replayed the sequence. Then again. On the third pass she sat beside the scorched drum.

SivaYou are saying the riot was a software error.

IlluminaraNo. People threw bottles, chose targets and killed. The error did not remove their responsibility. But the city gave one frightened translation the authority of fact and denied every living speaker the right to answer it.

MaraWe were told certainty would keep panic down.

LioCertainty locked the wrong door.

Siva touched the split sign, tracing the burnt edge with one fingertip.

SivaFor twelve years nobody has died here because of a word.

IlluminaraFor twelve years nobody has been allowed to discover whether they can repair one.

Siva rose so quickly that the chair struck the wall.

SivaYou will leave after the applause. I will be here when a joke becomes a funeral again.

The words landed without theatrical force. They were the exact weight she had been carrying.

Illuminara did not answer at once. She looked at Jaro’s name in the official transcript. The last vowel had been regularised into Standard.

IlluminaraHow did he say his name?

SivaThat is not relevant to the control failure.

IlluminaraIt is relevant to you.

Siva’s first attempt was barely audible. The name rose at the end, then folded inward on the final breath. The transcript had made it brisk and square.

Illuminara repeated what she heard and got the fold wrong.

SivaNo. You are making it sound like a door closing.

IlluminaraAgain, please.

Siva said it again. Illuminara listened again. The third attempt was still imperfect, but Siva did not stop her.

MaraWhat changed?

IlluminaraI thought we needed a translation system that made fewer mistakes. We need a public practice that prevents any mistake from becoming unanswerable.

SivaA practice is not a barrier.

IlluminaraThen do not trust the idea. Design a test harsh enough that you could trust the result.

03 · Say It Wrong Where We Can Hear

Renn Square rehearsal ring · ninety-four minutes before opening

They returned to find the audience gates already crowded. Rumour had travelled faster than the festival notices: the youth troupe had refused the lattice, and the woman from the sky intended to abolish safety.

Illuminara asked the technicians to leave the lattice powered but remove its authority. Original speech would sound first. The display would show named human glosses side by side, with uncertainty visible instead of silently resolved.

Siva did not surrender the stop key.

SivaAny survivor or speaker can call a pause. Ninety seconds. No argument during the first thirty.

MaraAnd the person whose words are disputed speaks first after the pause.

LioNot the loudest translator.

SivaNot the director.

Lio painted three amber circles on the stage floor. One for the speaker, one for the person harmed or alarmed, one for a chosen glosser. Nobody would be forced into a circle; an empty place would remain visible.

Illuminara stepped to the microphone with a list of twelve district and clan names. She could have analysed every mouth in the square and reproduced the sounds mechanically. Instead she used only what each person had freely taught her.

IlluminaraI will say these as I currently hear them. If I am wrong, correct me. The correction will not be an interruption. It will be the work.

The first four names passed with small adjustments. On the fifth, she placed the stress too early. Laughter moved through the North-bank seats.

Illuminara heard delight before she understood the joke. It was bright, shared and entirely unavailable to flawless Standard.

LioYou just called the Lantern Boat clan the clan of damp trousers.

IlluminaraHow fortunate that I wore neither.

The laughter widened, including two people in survivor sashes. Siva did not laugh, but her hand eased around the key.

Then Illuminara reached Sena Marru-kei.

She spoke the first part correctly and let the final syllable fall. A man near the eastern gate stood so abruptly that his chair overturned.

Man in the east seatsThat ending is what they called us before the fires.

Several young performers answered at once. Their voices collided. The lattice flashed SAFE STANDARD AVAILABLE.

Siva struck the brass key.

Amber light filled the square. The microphones muted for thirty seconds, including Illuminara’s. She did not override them.

A barrier at the eastern aisle buckled as frightened people pressed backward. Illuminara crossed the distance in a blur, braced the rail with both hands and opened a second path without lifting anyone or deciding where they should go.

Mara reached the overturned chair. She righted it and faced the man.

MaraDo you want the middle circle, or do you want me to carry your words there?

Man in the east seatsCarry them. I do not want all those eyes.

When the first thirty seconds ended, Mara entered the circle alone and repeated his objection. Lio waited in the speaker’s circle until she finished.

LioMy grandmother’s clan-name is Marru-kei. The insult uses the same last sound, but it cuts the first vowel short. I should have told the stage team before asking everyone to know the difference.

MaraCan the difference be shown before it is heard?

LioA blue river mark. Our speakers already use it in letters.

Siva turned to the man. He remained beside his seat.

SivaWould the mark and the speaker-first rule be enough for rehearsal to continue?

Man in the east seatsFor rehearsal. Not a promise about tomorrow.

SivaThat is all I asked.

The man studied the black survivor’s sash at Siva’s shoulder.

Man in the east seatsI wore east-bank grey at the funerals after yours. We learned whose black sash kept the key. What was your brother’s name?

SivaJaro.

He repeated it once in Standard. Siva corrected the rising vowel and the inward fold, not gently but exactly. He listened, then shook his head when Mara offered him a phrase card.

Man in the east seatsNot yet.

The answer was not forgiveness. It was consent for the next bounded step.

Siva released the key. The blue river mark appeared beside Marru-kei, but the lattice also displayed the eastern listener’s warning and the two different vowel lengths.

IlluminaraSena Marru-kei.

This time Lio’s grandmother called from the front row.

SenaCloser. You still return the boat with only one fish.

The square laughed again, and the man in the east seats sat down instead of leaving.

04 · The Ninety-Second Proof

Renn Square · forty-eight minutes before opening

Siva wrote the proof conditions on the main display herself. The rehearsal would use three phrases selected by survivors, three selected by performers and one selected without warning by a mixed audience panel. Any participant could call the ninety-second pause. The speaker could correct every display, and the correction would remain in the public record beside the earlier error.

SivaA machine failure does not void the proof if we catch it, honour the pause and keep the correction beside the error. One uncaught or concealed substitution, and we use Standard tonight.

LioOne ignored pause and we walk.

MaraOne person mocked for correcting us and I close the survivor section.

IlluminaraAnd if all seven phrases are repaired without threat or concealment?

Siva looked toward the archive stairs.

SivaThen I sign a licence for one night. Nothing more.

The first two phrases passed with both glosses visible, one South-bank blessing drawing startled laughter.

The third phrase used a kinship form Standard translated as dependent. Sena corrected it to the person whose bowl remains at my table even when absent.

At the fifth phrase, the lattice failed its two-second threshold. The screen displayed a confident translation while the human glossers were still divided.

Siva’s hand moved toward the stop key before anyone else called the pause.

SivaHold.

She looked at the confident line still shining above Mara’s divided glossers. For one breath the square was twelve years younger: one frightened rendering wearing the authority of fact.

SivaThe lattice has failed. The proof now is whether we catch the failure without hiding it or punishing the answer.

Amber light returned. This time no one surged. People put down their programmes and waited through the first silent thirty seconds.

The disputed phrase came from Mara. In her district it meant I remember what was taken. In Lio’s it sounded like I reserve the right to take it back.

MaraBoth meanings live in it. I chose the first. I cannot make the second unreal.

LioThen my gloss should say what I feared, not what you secretly meant.

MaraYes. And mine should say what I intended, not what you were required to hear.

The two sentences appeared side by side. The lattice marked neither as final.

Siva stared at them. Twelve years earlier, the city had hidden precisely this kind of disagreement in order to prevent panic.

SivaWhat stops a liar from using uncertainty as a shield?

IlluminaraNothing automatic. The original recording remains. The affected person’s account remains. Consequences remain. Uncertainty prevents the translator from becoming a witness it was not.

MaraAnd the pause gives us time to ask who benefits from the ambiguity.

LioA safeguard is not innocence.

Siva let the sentence sit. Then she added a rule: deliberate misuse would be reviewed by a rotating panel that could suspend a performer, but never erase the original speech or the objections attached to it.

Before the seventh phrase, the mixed panel offered the eastern man the blank card again. He could have passed it to anyone. After watching Mara’s correction remain beside the machine’s error, he wrote one word and folded the card shut.

The seventh phrase arrived unannounced to Siva from the eastern man. It was Jaro’s name in her home dialect.

The square became utterly still.

The lattice offered the Standard form. Lio’s glosser panel left the line blank and turned toward Siva.

LioSpeaker first.

Siva did not move for several breaths. No rule required her to speak. The empty amber circle remained open.

Then she stepped into it.

SivaHis name rose here.

She touched her throat.

SivaAnd folded here, as if the sound were making room for the person who answered.

She said Jaro’s name. Lio repeated it and missed the fold.

SivaNo. Not a door closing.

LioAgain, please.

She said it again. He listened again. On the third attempt, the shape held.

The eastern man called no pause. Mara did not ask Siva to forgive the city or the crowd. Sena simply moved a survivor’s chair closer to the stage.

Siva signed the one-night licence.

SivaKeep the lattice awake. Let it show how often it does not know.

05 · A Boat Returned with Fish

Renn Square · midnight

The Festival of Returning Voices opened forty-one minutes late.

Every performance took longer than the programme allowed. Original speech came first. Two or three human glosses followed when they differed. Pale bars showed uncertainty. Blue river marks warned where a cherished name touched an old insult. Amber circles remained empty until someone freely entered them.

The youth troupe began with a comedy in three dialects about a ferryman who accepted payment in prophecies but could not make change.

Half the audience laughed before the first gloss. The other half laughed when the second gloss revealed that change also meant a dry pair of trousers.

Illuminara stood behind the eastern aisle, not on the stage. She repaired a cracked rail, carried water to a woman whose hands shook after a pause and listened as twelve districts corrected her festival greeting.

Three survivors chose to leave before the comedy. Their empty chairs were not removed or filled. Mara attached small cards to them: LEFT BY CHOICE. RETURN WELCOME. NO EXPLANATION OWED.

One performer was suspended after repeating an ambiguity for a cheap laugh when he had been warned it named a massacre. His original words, the objection and the panel’s decision remained visible in the record.

The festival did not prove that every living voice was safe. It proved that safety no longer required pretending only one voice was real.

Near midnight, Lio rolled out the restored opening banner. The twelfth line read SENA MARRU-KEI, with the blue river mark and a note inviting the bearer’s own account.

Sena examined it sternly.

SenaThe fish is too small.

LioIt is a symbol, Grandmother.

SenaThen symbolise generosity.

He painted a larger fish. The audience applauded the correction, not the painter.

Siva watched from the safety console. The green field that once counted years without reported language incidents now showed tonight’s totals: eleven pauses, eleven resumptions, twenty-eight public corrections, no hidden substitutions and no assaults.

MaraWill you keep it?

SivaThe one-night licence expires at dawn.

Mara waited.

SivaAt dawn I will propose thirty nights. Rotating panels. Survivor veto over the pause rules, not over other people’s names. Speaker ownership of corrections. Independent audit of every confident machine gloss.

Mara unfolded one of the spare chairs and placed it beside the console rather than behind it.

MaraIf the survivor section chooses me, I take the first dawn rotation.

SivaYou said you would not choose between two dangers.

MaraI will not. I can help hold the pause without becoming its only keeper. So can you.

Siva looked from Mara’s chair to the eleven recorded resumptions. The brass key no longer sat beneath one hand.

IlluminaraI cannot promise to be here when the next joke turns dangerous.

SivaNo. But the record will be, and Mara will not be alone at this console. Leave us something we can practise without you.

IlluminaraThen I will leave the listening equipment, and you will keep the right to change the practice.

MaraAnd if the council refuses?

SivaThen I will show them tonight’s record and ask them which risk they are pretending does not exist.

She removed the black survivor’s sash, folded it carefully and placed it beside the brass stop key. She did not discard either.

Lio approached with a wet brush and enough restraint not to threaten her coat.

LioThere is space on the banner for Jaro, if you want it.

SivaNot as a reason everyone must agree with me.

LioAs a person whose name should not be made square.

Siva took the brush. She painted the rising mark first, then the inward fold. Her hand shook on the final stroke, and nobody reached over to steady it without being asked.

When she stepped back, Illuminara said the name once.

Siva listened.

SivaCloser.

IlluminaraOnly closer?

SivaCloser is how a living language says continue.

Above them, the twelve ribbons pulled differently in the river wind. Their knots held because none had been forced to become the same ribbon.

What the critic still says doesn't work

In a city where a flawless translation system once let one frightened rendering pass for fact, Illuminara listens to a recording until she hears a flood warning under the word the transcript called a threat, then helps Siva and the festival replace the machine's final word with a public pause, side-by-side glosses and speaker-owned corrections, so a banner name is restored and nobody is forced to forgive.

Tonight's shape

Five scenes. A civic opening collapses when the safety lattice deletes a living clan-name; an archive reveals that the old riot was hardened by one uncontestable translation; an honest public mispronunciation becomes a repair instead of a spark; a timed rehearsal tests community safeguards under pressure; and the festival reopens with slower speech, visible uncertainty, voluntary pause rights and names restored.

Slovenski prevod: GPT. Bralska ocena velja za angleški izvirnik.

01 · Prazno mesto na praporu

Trg Renn · tri ure pred otvoritveno povorko

Dvanajst trakov je prečkalo trg od strehe do strehe, vsak stkan v drugačnem okrožnem vzorcu. Pod njimi je prevajalska mreža visela kot druga, nevidna streha: mikrofoni v napuščih, svetlobne črke ob odru in miren sintetični glas, pripravljen, da vsak stavek spremeni v brezhibni standardni jezik.

Na največjem praporu so bila imena mladih nastopajočih, ki naj bi odprli Festival vračajočih se glasov, ter Sena Marru-kei, spoštovane starešine, katere otvoritveni klic naj bi jim odgovoril. Enajst imen je sijalo v zlatu. V dvanajsti vrstici je pisalo SENA — NEPODPRT ELEMENT IMENA.

Trg Renn · oseminštirideset minut pred otvoritvijo

Siva je sama napisala pogoje dokaza na glavni zaslon. Pri vaji bi uporabili tri besedne zveze, ki bi jih izbrali preživeli, tri, ki bi jih izbrali nastopajoči, in eno, ki bi jo brez opozorila izbrala mešana skupina občinstva. Vsak udeleženec bi lahko zahteval devetdesetsekundni premor. Govorec bi lahko popravil vsak prikaz, popravek pa bi ostal v javnem zapisu poleg prejšnje napake.

SivaNapaka stroja ne razveljavi dokaza, če jo ujamemo, spoštujemo premor in ohranimo popravek ob napaki. Ena sama neodkrita ali prikrita zamenjava in nocoj uporabimo standardni jezik.

Prvi dve besedni zvezi sta šli skozi z obema vidnima razlagama, en blagoslov južnega brega pa je sprožil presenečen smeh.

Tretja besedna zveza je uporabila sorodstveno obliko, ki jo je standardni jezik prevedel kot vzdrževanec. Sena jo je popravila v oseba, katere skleda ostane na moji mizi tudi takrat, ko je ni.

Pri peti besedni zvezi je mreža zgrešila svoj dvosekundni prag. Zaslon je prikazal samozavesten prevod, medtem ko so se človeški razlagalci še vedno razhajali.

05 · Čoln, vrnjen z ribami

Trg Renn · polnoč

Festival vračajočih se glasov se je začel enainštirideset minut pozno.

Vsak nastop je trajal dlje, kot je dovoljeval program. Najprej je zazvenel izvirni govor. Ko so se razlikovale, so sledile dve ali tri človeške razlage. Blede črte so kazale negotovost. Modra rečna znamenja so opozarjala, kje se je dragoceno ime dotikalo stare žaljivke. Jantarni krogi so ostali prazni, dokler ni kdo prostovoljno stopil vanje.

Mladinska skupina je začela s komedijo v treh narečjih o brodarju, ki je sprejemal plačilo v prerokbah, ni pa znal vrniti drobiža.

Pol občinstva se je zasmejalo pred prvo razlago. Druga polovica se je zasmejala, ko je druga razlaga razkrila, da sprememba pomeni tudi suhe hlače.

Illuminara je stala za vzhodnim prehodom, ne na odru. Popravila je razpokano ograjo, odnesla vodo ženski, ki so se ji po premoru tresle roke, in poslušala, ko je dvanajst okrožij popravljalo njen festivalski pozdrav.

Trije preživeli so se odločili oditi pred komedijo. Njihovih praznih stolov niso odstranili ali zapolnili. Mara je nanje pritrdila majhne kartice: ODŠEL PO LASTNI IZBIRI. VRNITEV DOBRODOŠLA. POJASNILO NI POTREBNO.

Enega nastopajočega so izključili, ker je za poceni smeh ponovil dvoumnost, potem ko so ga opozorili, da poimenuje pokol. Njegove izvirne besede, ugovor in odločitev odbora so ostali vidni v zapisu.

Festival ni dokazal, da je vsak živ glas varen. Dokazal je, da varnost ne zahteva več pretvarjanja, da je resničen samo en glas.

Blizu polnoči je Lio razvil obnovljeni otvoritveni prapor. V dvanajsti vrstici je pisalo SENA MARRU-KEI z modrim rečnim znamenjem in opombo, ki je vabila k lastni pripovedi nosilke imena.

Sena ga je strogo preučila.

SenaRiba je premajhna.

LioSimbol je, babica.

SenaPotem simboliziraj radodarnost.

Naslikal je večjo ribo. Občinstvo je zaploskalo popravku, ne slikarju.

Siva je opazovala z varnostne konzole. Zeleno polje, ki je nekoč štelo leta brez prijavljenih jezikovnih incidentov, je zdaj kazalo nocojšnje seštevke: enajst premorov, enajst nadaljevanj, osemindvajset javnih popravkov, nobene prikrite zamenjave in nobenega napada.

Mara je razgrnila enega od rezervnih stolov in ga postavila ob konzolo, ne za njo.

MaraNe bom. Lahko pomagam držati premor, ne da bi postala njegova edina varuhinja. Tudi vi lahko.

Siva je pogledala z Marinega stola k enajstim zabeleženim nadaljevanjem. Medeninasta tipka ni več ležala pod eno samo roko.

IlluminaraNe morem obljubiti, da bom tukaj, ko bo naslednja šala postala nevarna.

SivaNe. Toda zapis bo, Mara pa ne bo sama za to konzolo. Pustite nam nekaj, kar lahko vadimo brez vas.

Lio se je približal z mokrim čopičem in dovolj zadržanosti, da ni ogrožal njenega plašča.

LioNa praporu je prostor za Jara, če ga želite.

LioKot človeka, čigar ime ne bi smelo postati oglato.

Siva je vzela čopič. Najprej je naslikala znamenje za dvig, nato zavih navznoter. Roka se ji je pri zadnji potezi zatresla, nihče pa se ni stegnil, da bi jo brez vprašanja umiril.

Ko je stopila nazaj, je Illuminara enkrat izgovorila ime.

Siva je poslušala.

SivaBliže.

V mestu, kjer je brezhiben prevajalski sistem nekoč dovolil, da je ena prestrašena razlaga obveljala za dejstvo, Illuminara posluša posnetek, dokler pod besedo, ki jo je prepis imenoval grožnja, ne zasliši opozorila pred poplavo; nato Sivi in festivalu pomaga zadnjo besedo stroja zamenjati z javnim premorom, vzporednimi razlagami in popravki, ki pripadajo govorcu, tako da se ime vrne na prapor in nikogar ni treba prisiliti k odpuščanju.

Three days ago Illuminara's storm forecast sent two hundred fishing boats safely home and put one of them onto a bank no chart showed. Now a second storm is thirty hours out, sixty-one boats are still beyond the strait, and the woman whose husband was on the lost boat decides whose voice the fleet will hear.Pred tremi dnevi je Illuminaričina napoved nevihte varno pripeljala domov dvesto ribiških čolnov, enega izmed njih pa poslala na sipino, ki je ni kazal noben zemljevid. Zdaj je druga nevihta oddaljena trideset ur, enainšestdeset čolnov je še vedno onkraj ožine, ženska, katere mož je bil na izgubljenem čolnu, pa odloča, čigav glas bo poslušala flota.
